title: Bito Soup
localName: Bito — bira, biire, hibiscus leaf soup
author: Northern Ghanaian tradition
desc: Hibiscus leaf with groundnut paste and locust bean — the only quantified version in print is brand marketing, and it contradicts itself.
longDesc: Bito is the sour hibiscus leaf of northern Ghana — bito to the Frafra, bira to the Dagomba — and the soup made from it uses groundnut paste and dawadawa. Only one source publishes quantities and it is a seasoning brand's marketing page, which also contradicts itself: its ingredient list says spinach while its method says shuure leaves, and it describes the dish as containing hibiscus leaves while calling it parsley peanut soup. All of that is flagged below. Four tablespoons of groundnut paste, two of locust beans, a teaspoon of grains of paradise, and about forty minutes.
ingredients: Beef, cut for stewing — no quantity is printed
1 bunch bito (hibiscus) leaves — the source prints spinach, see the note
steps: Simmer the beef with the shallots, garlic, ginger, grains of paradise and thyme for 15 minutes.
Add the groundnut paste mixture and cook 5 minutes.
Add the leaves, the dawadawa and the seasoning tablet.
Stir and let simmer for 3 minutes.
chefTips: Bito is hibiscus leaf — Hibiscus sabdariffa, the same plant as sobolo — and it is sour rather than slimy. That is what distinguishes bito soup from ayoyo.
Groundnut paste and dawadawa together are the northern leaf-soup formula, documented by the 1968 government survey as well as by the modern sources.
Grains of paradise, a teaspoon, is a genuinely northern aromatic and worth sourcing.

Be aware the only quantified version is a brand's marketing page, it substitutes spinach for the hibiscus leaf in its ingredient list, and its method names a third leaf entirely. Use real bito if you can get it.
The dawadawa and the leaves go in near the END, for three minutes only. Long boiling flattens both.
The beef carries no quantity at all in the source. Six hundred grams for six servings is a reasonable reading, offered as such.
An ethnographic study describes bra soup as prepared like light soup with groundnut paste and bra leaves, which is a plainer and probably more typical version than this one.
commonMistakes: Using spinach and expecting bito's sourness.
Boiling the leaves and dawadawa for a long time.
Leaving out the groundnut paste, which is structural.
Substituting black pepper for grains of paradise.
Treating the brand page's quantities as authoritative.
sources: SOURCING FLAG STATED FIRST, because it governs everything below: THE ONLY SOURCE THAT PUBLISHES QUANTITIES FOR BITO SOUP IS BRAND MARKETING. Quantities adapted from 'BITTO' on maggi.com.gh, credited to 'MAGGI Ghana'. Yield as printed: 6 servings, 40 minutes. It is a seasoning manufacturer's recipe page and it fails this collection's named-author bar; it is used because NO ACCEPTED RECIPE WITH QUANTITIES EXISTS ANYWHERE ELSE for this dish, and everything taken from it is flagged.

Ingredients exactly as printed, confirmed across two fetches: 'Beef, New Zealand, imported, manufacturing beef, raw' (NO QUANTITY); Shallots 0.5 cup; Garlic 5 cloves; Ginger (Chopped) 1 small; grains of paradise 1 tsp; Thyme 1 tsp; MAGGI DƐDƐƐDƐ 2; Groundnut Paste 4 tbsp; Tomato Paste 1 tbsp; Spinach (Kontomire) 1 bunch; Locust Beans 2 tbsp; Fresh Pepper 4. The brand name is rendered generically as seasoning tablets above.

Method as printed: simmer 15 min; groundnut mix 5 min; then 'Allow to simmer for 10 minutes then add the shuure leaves, dawadawa, MAGGI d3d33d3 tablet. Stir and let simmer for 3 minutes then add scotch bonnet pepper.'

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION, flagged and NOT corrected: the INGREDIENT LIST says SPINACH (Kontomire) while the METHOD says 'shuure leaves'. Those are different plants. The page separately describes the dish as having 'hibiscus leaves in it' and calls it a 'traditional northern region recipe, also called parsley peanut soup or biire'. So the page names FOUR different leaves across its own text — spinach, shuure, hibiscus and parsley — and resolves none of them. The ingredient list above prints bito with a pointer to this note, because the botanical identification below is firmer than the brand page's.

THE BOTANY, which is the one firm thing here. Whitby 1968, 'Foods of Ghana', FRI Research Bulletin No. 1, verbatim: 'Sour-sour; Guinea sorrel. Hibiscus sabdariffa. Bito (Frafra) Bira (Dagomba). This is one of the commonest leafy vegetables. The seeds..., pods and flower-calyces are also used for food.' So bito is HIBISCUS LEAF, not parsley and not spinach. The brand page's 'parsley peanut soup' is UNRECONCILED with this and the Whitby identification is preferred for the community and the local-name fields.

A PLAINER DESCRIPTION, from the GAIN 2016 focused ethnographic study of Karaga District, authors Margaret Armar-Klemesu, Sawudatu Zakariah-Akoto and Sarah Osei-Menya, verbatim: 'Bra soup: Prepared similar to light soup but with added groundnut paste and/or pounded raw groundnuts and bra leaves.' That is probably closer to the everyday dish than the brand recipe, but it carries NO QUANTITIES.

THE NORTHERN LEAF-SOUP FORMULA, from Whitby 1968: 'These soups may include groundnut paste or dawadawa (fermented locust bean) or kantong (other fermented oil seeds).' Groundnut paste plus dawadawa is therefore documented as the regional pattern across sixty years.
NO DONENESS CUE of any kind is printed on the brand page — only the times.
THE BEEF QUANTITY IS GENUINELY ABSENT and no figure has been asserted; the six hundred grams in the tips is explicitly labelled as a reading.

WHY THIS IS PUBLISHED DESPITE ALL OF THAT: bito is one of the commonest leafy vegetables in northern Ghana by the government survey's own account, and the alternative is to leave it out entirely. Publishing it with the leaf confusion, the missing beef weight and the brand provenance all stated is more useful than silence — but a reader should treat these quantities as the weakest in the Ghanaian set alongside GHA060.
healthBenefits: Hibiscus leaf is high in vitamin C, calcium and iron.
Groundnut paste supplies plant protein, niacin and vitamin E.
Dawadawa is a fermented food with documented B-vitamin content.
Grains of paradise carry documented antimicrobial compounds.
culturalNote: Bito is sour where ayoyo is slippery, and the two are the alternating leaf soups of a northern Ghanaian week. That the only written quantities for one of the region's commonest dishes come from a stock-cube advertisement is the clearest single illustration of how unevenly Ghanaian food has been documented.
